title: Inverse Design for Conditional Distribution Matching

paper.title: Inverse Design for Conditional Distribution Matching
paper.abstract:
Abstract Generative models are powerful tools for sampling from a learned distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) , and inverse-design methods invert this map to find an input x x that produces a desired point output y ∗ y^{*} . However, many design goals are naturally distributional rather than pointwise, incorporating the inherent uncertainty of Y Y and targeting a specific form for it, a task not addressed by standard inverse design.
To address this issue we introduce Conditional Distribution Matching
(CDM) 1 1 1 The phrase ”conditional distribution matching” is also used in the domain-adaptation literature [ 41 ] with a different meaning (aligning source and target conditionals
across datasets); our use is an inverse-design problem over a fixed generative process. See Section 3 for details. ,
a new inverse-design problem class in generative modeling: given a joint distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{P}(X,Y) and a target distribution 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) ,
find an input x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional
distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . We formally define two variants: Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (CDMS) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (CDMO). To solve these problems, we propose MLGD-F ( Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion
with a Fast inner sampler ), a plug-and-play inference-time algorithm that combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. By leveraging single-step conditional sampling, MLGD-F enables tractable gradient computation, making the estimation of 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) both memory-efficient and computationally lightweight. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic benchmarks, structured image transformations, and generative editing optimization, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank supports.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models have emerged as a cornerstone of modern machine learning, achieving remarkable results in image synthesis, voice generation, and time-series modeling [ 19 , 43 , 39 ] . The paradigm has evolved from unconditional generation , learning to sample from an unknown data distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) [ 33 , 16 , 34 ] , toward increasingly controlled generation. Conditional generation allows sampling x 0 ∼ 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ∣ Y = y ) x_{0}\sim\mathcal{P}(X\mid Y=y) for a user-specified label y y [ 9 , 17 ] , loss-guided methods [ 6 , 35 ] generate samples that minimize a given objective ℒ : 𝒳 → ℝ \mathcal{L}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} while remaining faithful to the data distribution. A natural instantiation of loss-guided generation is inverse design : find an input x x such that a forward learned model f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) is close to a desired point output y ∗ y^{*} [ 31 ] , successfully applied in protein engineering [ 8 ] and drug discovery [ 13 ] . However, this paradigm is inherently limited to point targets: it cannot express goals where the desired outcome is a distribution over outputs rather than a single value. In many modern settings the mapping from input to output is mediated by a complex generative process 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) that we cannot modify: a pretrained diffusion model with billions of parameters, a physical process such as protein folding, or a black-box simulator. The only lever the user controls is the input x x . Classical inverse design uses this lever to match a specific target output y ∗ y^{*} : find x x such that f ⁡ ( x ) ≈ y ∗ f(x)\approx y^{*} . In many applications, however, the desired outcome is not a single value but a distribution over outcomes, for instance, an amino acid sequence x x such that 𝒫 ⁡ ( structure ∣ X = x ) ≈ 1 2 ​ δ A + 1 2 ​ δ B \mathcal{P}(\text{structure}\mid X=x)\approx\frac{1}{2}\delta_{A}+\frac{1}{2}\delta_{B} for two target folds A A and B B [ 15 ] , generative pipelines whose outputs are balanced across demographic groups, or design tasks that require diverse but constrained outputs. We address the more general distributional inverse-design problem: accept any frozen 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) , optimise the controllable input x x , and target a user-specified distribution 𝒢 \mathcal{G} over Y Y rather than a point y ∗ y^{*} , without relying on domain-specific scoring functions.

sections.heading: Our contributions.
sections.text: 1. Problem formulation. We define two problems, Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (Problem 1 ) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (Problem 2 ), which move beyond characterizing samples by their own properties, instead seeking x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) . 2. Algorithm. MLGD-F combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler to enable tractable gradient-based optimisation through single-step conditional sampling, operating entirely at inference time with no fine-tuning. 3. Empirical validation. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic Mixture of Gaussians, an MNIST rotation task, and a large-scale Stable Diffusion image editing pipeline, demonstrating recovery of inputs whose induced conditional distributions match user-specified targets.

sections.heading: 2 Problem Formulation
sections.text: We consider a joint distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{P}(X,Y) over paired random variables, where X X denotes a variable of interest and Y Y an associated variable. Let ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denote a distance metric between probability distributions (e.g., the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, MMD, or the Sliced Wasserstein Distance, SWD). Problem 1 (Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling) . Given a target distribution 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) , the ideal target is the tilted distribution 𝒬 β ​ ( x ) ∝ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ) ​ e − β ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) , where ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ , \mathcal{Q}_{\beta}(x)\propto\mathcal{P}(x)\,e^{-\beta\,\mathcal{L}(x)},\quad\text{where}\quad\mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\|, with β ≥ 0 \beta\!\geq\!0 an inverse temperature interpolating between the prior ( β = 0 \beta\!=\!0 ) and the optimum of ℒ \mathcal{L} ( β → ∞ \beta\!\to\!\infty ). Exact sampling from 𝒬 β \mathcal{Q}_{\beta} requires an intractable noisy-time guidance score; our algorithm (Section 4 ) provides an LGD-style approximate sampler, analysed in Remark 2 of Appendix E . Problem 2 (Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization) . Find input x ∗ x^{*} that minimizes the distance between the induced conditional distribution and the target: x ∗ ≡ arg ⁡ min x ​ ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ . x^{*}\;\equiv\;\arg\min_{x}\;\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\|. Problem 2 corresponds to Problem 1 in the limit β → ∞ \beta\to\infty , where 𝒬 ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{Q}(x) concentrates at the mode of the loss. Both problems are instances of loss-guided sampling [ 35 ] specialised to the distributional loss ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ \mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\| .

sections.heading: Diffusion models.
sections.text: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [ 33 , 16 ] define a forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data x 0 x_{0} over T T steps, producing a sequence x 0 , x 1 , … , x T x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{T} , and learn a reverse process that denoises x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) back to a sample x 0 x_{0} from the data distribution. Throughout we use this notation: x t x_{t} is the noisy state at timestep t t ; the forward marginal has the closed form q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = α ¯ t ​ x 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and noise schedule { α ¯ t } t = 1 T \{\bar{\alpha}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} ; s θ ​ ( x t , t ) s_{\theta}(x_{t},t) denotes the learned score network of the unconditional model for 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) ; and x ^ 0 = ( x t + ( 1 − α ¯ t ) ​ s θ ​ ( x t , t ) ) / α ¯ t \hat{x}_{0}\!=\!(x_{t}+(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})s_{\theta}(x_{t},t))/\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}} is Tweedie’s estimate of the clean sample given x t x_{t} . Score-based models [ 38 ] provide a unifying SDE framework for this family. A deterministic alternative to ancestral sampling is the probability flow ODE (used via the DDIM sampler [ 34 ] ), which traces a deterministic trajectory through the same marginals and enables faster sampling with fewer steps.

sections.heading: Few-step diffusion models.
sections.text: Standard diffusion models require 30 30 – 1000 1000 sequential denoising steps at inference time [ 16 , 34 ] , motivating research into faster inference strategies. One direction is consistency models [ 36 , 37 ] , which enforce self-consistency along the probability-flow ODE trajectory without requiring a pretrained teacher. Another direction is diffusion distillation , which compresses a pretrained diffusion model into a student that generates samples in one or very few steps [ 30 , 32 ] . We exploit the single-step property common to both families to make inner-loop conditional sampling tractable at every denoising step of the outer diffusion process.

sections.heading: Loss-guided sampling.
sections.text: Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) [ 6 ] and Loss-Guided Diffusion (LGD) [ 35 ] modify the reverse diffusion process by incorporating gradient information from a differentiable loss function ℒ ⁡ ( x 0 ) \mathcal{L}(x_{0}) . At each denoising step, the score is augmented by ∇ x t ℒ ​ ( x ^ 0 ) \nabla_{x_{t}}\mathcal{L}(\hat{x}_{0}) , where x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is an estimate of the clean sample obtained via Tweedie’s formula. LGD further stabilises the gradient by averaging over multiple Monte Carlo Tweedie estimates. This framework enables flexible, zero-shot guidance for a wide range of objectives without retraining the generative prior.

sections.heading: Distribution matching.
sections.text: A large family of generative methods trains a parametric generator so that its output distribution matches a target 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , using losses based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy [ 22 , 21 ] , Optimal Transport / Sinkhorn divergences [ 12 ] , These approaches require differentiating through the generator and updating its weights, making them expensive and target-specific: a new 𝒢 \mathcal{G} requires retraining. Our setting is orthogonal: the generative pipeline (both the diffusion prior and the conditional model f ϕ f_{\phi} ) is frozen , and we instead optimise a single input x ∗ x^{*} such that 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . No generator weights are updated, no target-specific training is required, and the method operates entirely at inference time.

sections.heading: Terminological note.
sections.text: The phrase "conditional distribution matching" has prior unrelated uses. In the domain-adaptation literature [ 41 ] it refers to aligning the source and target conditionals 𝒫 src ​ ( X ∣ Y ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{src}}(X\mid Y) and 𝒫 tgt ​ ( X ∣ Y ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tgt}}(X\mid Y) across two datasets so that a classifier learned on one transfers to the other. In concurrent work on discrete-diffusion distillation [ 11 ] it refers to a training objective in which a student model is trained to match a pretrained teacher’s reverse conditional transitions. Our use is unrelated to either: we study the inverse-design problem of finding an input x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) , with a single fixed generative process. The three problems share only a phrase, not a setup or method.

sections.heading: 4 Methodology
sections.text: MLGD (Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion) specialises Loss-Guided Diffusion [ 35 ] to the conditional distribution matching setting (Problems 1 – 2 ) by combining the pretrained score network s θ s_{\theta} for 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) with a conditional sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} for 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) . When f ϕ f_{\phi} is a few-step sampler, we refer to the instantiation as MLGD-F; MLGD is the broader framework that also covers slower choices of f ϕ f_{\phi} . The method has two components: an outer loop that performs loss-guided reverse diffusion with a black-box loss ℒ ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{L}(x) (the LGD skeleton), and an inner estimator that evaluates and differentiates the distribution-matching loss ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ \mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\| at each outer step. The inner estimator is the paper’s algorithmic contribution.

sections.heading: 4.1 Inner estimator: discussion
sections.text: We refer to any fast, few-step, differentiable conditional sampler used as f ϕ f_{\phi} generically; in the synthetic and MNIST experiments this is a consistency model, while in the Stable Diffusion pipeline we use SDXL-Turbo [ 32 ] , which shares the same key property of single-step sampling. The loss ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ \mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\| cannot be evaluated analytically because 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x) is unknown: neither its density nor a way to enumerate it is available; we have only a pretrained sampler. Algorithm 2 bypasses this by plug-in estimation, then relies on autograd through f ϕ f_{\phi} for the gradient.

sections.heading: Why a fast sampler.
sections.text: The choice of a fast model for f ϕ f_{\phi} is deliberate. Because the inner estimator is invoked at every one of the T T outer denoising steps, a standard K ⋆ K_{\star} -step diffusion model would multiply the sampling cost by T ⋅ K ⋆ ⋅ n cond T\cdot K_{\star}\cdot n_{\mathrm{cond}} and, more critically, would require backpropagating through a K ⋆ K_{\star} -step unrolled chain at each outer step, rendering gradient computation memory-intensive and effectively intractable. A single-step f ϕ f_{\phi} ( K s = 1 K_{s}{=}1 ) keeps both cost and activation memory lightweight; we measure the resulting memory gap in Section 5.4 .

sections.heading: Sampling vs. optimisation, and the role of β \beta .
sections.text: Algorithm 1 interpolates between two regimes controlled by the inverse temperature β \beta of the target 𝒬 β ​ ( x ) ∝ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ) ​ e − β ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) \mathcal{Q}_{\beta}(x)\propto\mathcal{P}(x)\,e^{-\beta\mathcal{L}(x)} (Problem 1 ). At β = 0 \beta=0 the guidance vanishes and the algorithm draws approximate samples from the prior 𝒫 \mathcal{P} ; as β → ∞ \beta\to\infty it concentrates at arg ⁡ min x ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) \arg\min_{x}\mathcal{L}(x) , recovering the optimisation variant (Problem 2 ). In practice, β \beta can be absorbed into the step-size schedule by setting ζ t ← β ​ ζ t \zeta_{t}\leftarrow\beta\,\zeta_{t} , so the two are not separately identified. Following LGD, the trajectory targets 𝒬 β \mathcal{Q}_{\beta} only approximately (the exact noisy-time guidance score is intractable); Remark 2 in Appendix E states the approximation explicitly. In practice we report CDMO solutions by running at large β \beta with R R independent restarts x T ( r ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}^{(r)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and returning x ∗ = arg ⁡ min r = 1 , … , R ​ ℒ ^ ​ ( x 0 ( r ) ) x^{*}=\arg\min_{r=1,\ldots,R}\,\widehat{\mathcal{L}}(x_{0}^{(r)}) .

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments address two core properties of MLGD-F: its capacity to optimize over high-dimensional input manifolds X X , and its scalability to semantically complex output spaces Y Y . We evaluate across three settings of increasing scale: synthetic Mixture of Gaussians (Section 5.1 ), where low-dimensional X X and Y Y allow verification against known ground-truth optima; an MNIST rotation task (Section 5.2 ), which scales X X to image space ( ℝ 784 \mathbb{R}^{784} ) while keeping Y Y small; and a Stable Diffusion image optimization (Section 5.3 ), which scales both X X and Y Y to high-dimensional spaces.

sections.heading: 5.1 Synthetic Simulations
sections.text: We compare MLGD-F against MLGD with a slow diffusion sampler on Mixture of Gaussians across multiple dimensionalities. We run 25 optimisation instances and select the top-10 by final loss (Problem 2 ). Reporting top- k k reflects how multistart optimisation is used in practice: a user running R R restarts returns the best result by the same objective, so top- k k captures achievable quality under finite restart budgets. We also report all-25 statistics to characterise variance across seeds. Full models and training details are provided in Appendix A . As shown in Figure 1 , MLGD-F recovers near-optimal solutions with an 11 × 11\times speedup over MLGD ( 4.03 4.03 s vs. 45.58 45.58 s for the representative run shown; full per-dimensionality timing across all 25 runs is reported in Appendix A ). Notably, ECDF analysis (Figure 4 ) reveals that MLGD-F’s relative performance improves with dimensionality. We attribute this to the trade-off between sampler fidelity and gradient variance : while MLGD with a slow sampler uses a more accurate conditional model, backpropagating through its unrolled K ⋆ K_{\star} -step chain accumulates variance that scales poorly with dimension. MLGD-F’s single-step model provides a cleaner gradient signal, which becomes the decisive factor in high-dimensional settings (Appendix A.8 ). The β \beta -sweep in Figure 1 (bottom) empirically illustrates the sampling-to-optimisation interpolation of Problem 1 : as β \beta increases from 0 0 to large values, MLGD-F transitions from sampling the prior 𝒫 \mathcal{P} to concentrating near arg ⁡ min x ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) \arg\min_{x}\mathcal{L}(x) . sections.heading: 5.2 MNIST: Rotated Digits
sections.text: We apply MLGD-F to an image-space problem using the MNIST dataset [ 20 ] , where X ∈ ℝ 784 X\in\mathbb{R}^{784} is a digit image and Y ∈ ℝ 2 Y\in\mathbb{R}^{2} is its rotation angle encoded as ( cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ ) (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) ; a standard diffusion model serves as 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) and a consistency model as f ϕ f_{\phi} for 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) . The goal is to find x ∗ x^{*} such that 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) ≈ 𝒢 \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*})\approx\mathcal{G} for various user-specified target distributions 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . Since the unconditional model can generate any digit at any orientation, the optimization searches over the full joint space of digit identity and rotation. We present the top-5 results by final loss across 15 runs (Figure 2 , and Table 1 ); full qualitative results are provided in Appendix B.6 . These runs are approximate samples from the β \beta -tempered posterior 𝒬 β ​ ( x ) ∝ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ) ​ e − β ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) \mathcal{Q}_{\beta}(x)\propto\mathcal{P}(x)e^{-\beta\mathcal{L}(x)} (Problem 1 ), and the digit-class distribution in Table 1 is the empirical realisation of this posterior. While the objective is distributional and agnostic to digit identity, MLGD-F recovers semantically coherent digits that satisfy the orientation constraint 𝒢 \mathcal{G} : symmetric digits dominate under the uniform target (digit 0) and bimodal target (narrow 0, 1, 8, 6, 9), while oriented digits (2, 3, 7) emerge under the unimodal target. sections.heading: 5.3 Stable Diffusion: Distribution-Guided Image Generation
sections.text: To demonstrate scalability to large pretrained models, we apply MLGD-F to image editing with SDXL [ 28 ] , which serves as 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) ; SDXL-Turbo [ 32 ] serves as the fast conditional sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} for 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) . All targets are defined in CLIP [ 29 ] embedding space. We define four distribution matching tasks chosen to cover qualitatively distinct target shapes ranging from discrete mixtures to continuous low-rank support: (i) Balanced ( 𝒢 b ​ a ​ l \mathcal{G}_{bal} ): 0.5 ⋅ δ male + 0.5 ⋅ δ female 0.5\cdot\delta_{\text{male}}+0.5\cdot\delta_{\text{female}} , an equal-weight two-mode mixture. (ii) Skewed ( 𝒢 s ​ k ​ e ​ w \mathcal{G}_{skew} ): 0.25 ⋅ δ male + 0.75 ⋅ δ female 0.25\cdot\delta_{\text{male}}+0.75\cdot\delta_{\text{female}} , an unequal-weight two-mode mixture. (iii) Gender interpolation ( 𝒢 i ​ n ​ t ​ e ​ r ​ p ​ G ​ e ​ n ​ d ​ e ​ r \mathcal{G}_{interpGender} ): supported on a one-dimensional feminine-to-masculine continuum, approximated by four anchor classes. (iv) Age interpolation ( 𝒢 i ​ n ​ t ​ e ​ r ​ p ​ A ​ g ​ e \mathcal{G}_{interpAge} ): supported on a one-dimensional age continuum over male portraits, via prompts “a portrait of a { age } -year-old man” with uniform age distribution. Full construction details are provided in Appendix C . Together, these targets demonstrate the method’s target-shape generality: discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank submanifolds of output space are handled by the same algorithm without modification. The objective is to ensure the edited scribble x ∗ x^{*} satisfies 𝒫 ⁡ ( gender ∣ scribble = x ∗ ) ≈ 𝒢 \mathcal{P}(\text{gender}\mid\text{scribble}=x^{*})\approx\mathcal{G} .

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: Starting from a male portrait scribble (e.g. Figure 3 ), we employ SDEdit [ 26 ] to partially noise the image and denoise it, using MLGD-F as the guidance signal during the reverse diffusion trajectory. Concretely, line 1 of Algorithm 1 is replaced: rather than initialising from pure Gaussian noise x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , we start from a partially noised version of the source scribble; all subsequent steps of Algorithm 1 are unchanged. At each denoising step, the predicted clean latent x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is decoded into a scribble and passed to ControlNet-Scribble [ 44 ] for conditional image generation; example outputs are shown in Figure 3 . The resulting images are embedded via CLIP ViT-L/14 [ 29 ] and compared against the target distribution 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . MLGD-F requires 171–241 minutes of wall-clock time depending on the hyperparameters. We compare MLGD-F against two baselines: ( i ) Average scribble : pixel-wise weighted mean of HED maps [ 44 ] from generated male and female portraits (e.g., 0.25 ⋅ HED male + 0.75 ⋅ HED female 0.25{\cdot}\text{HED}_{\text{male}}+0.75{\cdot}\text{HED}_{\text{female}} ); ( ii ) SDEdit Best : unguided SDEdit applied repeatedly to the source scribble; the candidate minimising MMD against 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is selected, with the number of candidates chosen so that SDEdit’s total runtime matches MLGD-F’s wall-clock time.

sections.heading: 5.4 Ablation Study: Necessity of distilled Models
sections.text: We validate that few-step models (e.g., SDXL Turbo [ 32 ] ) are essential for tractable optimization by comparing our approach against standard diffusion-based inner-loop sampling. The memory gap is formalised by Proposition 3 in Appendix E : the few-step student reduces reverse-mode graph depth by the step-count ratio K ⋆ / K s K_{\star}/K_{s} , with the resulting student-teacher gradient discrepancy controlled by the additional distillation errors O ⁡ ( ε g , dist + ε dist ) O(\varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dist}}) .

sections.heading: Architectural Parity and Scaling.
sections.text: To isolate the impact of the denoising step count, we observe that our setup utilizes an identical architectural backbone across both configurations: the UNet ( ≈ \approx 2.6B parameters), ControlNet [ 44 ] , and CLIP text encoders [ 29 ] remain constant. Notably, SDXL-Turbo is obtained by distilling SDXL-Base with the architecture unchanged - the two models differ only in their weights, not their structure [ 32 ] . Consequently, the computational cost of a single forward pass is equivalent across both, and all observed differences in memory and speed are a direct consequence of the denoising step count alone. The observed differences in memory and speed are thus a direct consequence of the computation graph depth. Since SDXL Base requires K ⋆ = 30 K_{\star}=30 steps for high-quality reconstruction compared to K s = 2 K_{s}=2 for SDXL Turbo, the resulting gradient graph is fundamentally 15 × 15\times deeper. To manage memory, one can employ gradient checkpointing ; however, while this technique avoids storing intermediate activations, the overhead of maintaining the computation graph nodes for each of the K K denoising steps still scales linearly with the number of iterations.

sections.heading: Memory Tractability.
sections.text: At each outer denoising step, our method generates n cond n_{\text{cond}} conditional samples whose gradient graph must remain resident in GPU memory until autograd.grad is invoked. The peak memory cost decomposes as: M peak = M models + M fixed + n cond ⋅ M var ​ ( K ) M_{\text{peak}}=M_{\text{models}}+M_{\text{fixed}}+n_{\text{cond}}\cdot M_{\text{var}}(K) (1) where M models M_{\text{models}} is the static model weight footprint, M fixed M_{\text{fixed}} is the unconditional forward pass cost, and M var ​ ( K ) M_{\text{var}}(K) is the per-sample graph cost for a sampler with K K inner denoising steps. Since the autograd engine must track all unrolled iterations, total memory is Θ ⁡ ( n cond ⋅ K ) \Theta(n_{\text{cond}}\cdot K) . For the Stable Diffusion experiment (Section 5.3 ), we measured peak memory empirically on an NVIDIA A100 (80 GB variant) using n cond = 100 n_{\text{cond}}=100 conditional samples per step (the main optimization runs reported in Appendix C.7 were executed on an NVIDIA L40S; the A100 was used for the memory ablation and final validation on 2,000 2{,}000 samples): • SDXL Turbo ( K s = 2 K_{s}=2 ): The full pipeline consumes 43 GB peak VRAM. • SDXL Base ( K ⋆ = 30 K_{\star}=30 ): Replacing the sampler with the base model, we project a peak memory requirement of approximately 375 GB ( exceeding available hardware capacity by 4.4 × \times ), making the method entirely infeasible.

sections.heading: Temporal Efficiency.
sections.text: Beyond memory, the distilled model provides a critical speedup. For a run of 125 steps with n c ​ o ​ n ​ d = 100 n_{cond}=100 variations, the Turbo-based pipeline requires approximately 4 hr , compared to projected 52 hr for the Base-based pipeline. This order-of-magnitude reduction transforms MLGD-F into a tractable tool for iterative research and deployment.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM) , a new problem class that generalizes inverse design to the distributional setting. Rather than seeking an input x x that produces a specific output y ∗ y^{*} , CDM seeks an input x ∗ x^{*} whose entire induced conditional distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) . To our knowledge, this problem class has not been explicitly studied before. We formalized two variants, CDMS and CDMO, and introduced MLGD-F to solve them at inference time without any training or fine-tuning. A central advantage of the plug-and-play design is that MLGD-F directly inherits quality gains from improvements in the underlying pretrained models: as stronger diffusion priors and few-step conditional samplers become available, optimization quality improves automatically. The few-step model is essential for tractability: as demonstrated in Section 5.4 , replacing a single-step sampler with a standard multi-step diffusion model increases peak memory by nearly an order of magnitude and runtime from hours to days, rendering the method infeasible at scale. Empirically, we validated MLGD-F across settings of increasing scale and complexity, from synthetic Mixture of Gaussians, through an MNIST rotation task, to a large-scale Stable Diffusion image editing pipeline, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose induced conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank submanifolds.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Optimization quality is bounded by the fidelity of the pretrained distilled model — if the conditional sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} poorly approximates 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) , the guidance gradient will be biased regardless of the number of runs. The stochastic nature of the inner-loop loss estimation means multiple independent runs are often needed to find a good solution, which multiplies the compute cost. Runtime at large scale may be prohibitive for latency-sensitive applications. Finally, the method currently requires the conditional model to be differentiable end-to-end with respect to the input x x ; non-differentiable or black-box conditional models would require gradient-free extensions.

sections.heading: Future Work.
sections.text: CDM opens a research direction of optimizing over induced conditional distributions, one we hope will inspire dedicated solvers, tighter theoretical guarantees, and new application domains. This work focuses on continuous input spaces; an important direction is extending CDM to discrete spaces. A complementary direction is replacing the LGD-style approximate sampler (Remark 2 ) by an asymptotically exact corrector for the outer loop, twisted SMC, MCMC, or Feynman–Kac reweighting, to obtain 𝒬 β \mathcal{Q}_{\beta} samples with quantifiable bias at the cost of extra compute. Finally, an intriguing question is whether few-step samplers offer advantages beyond speed: their single-step structure may yield cleaner gradient signals compared to unrolled multi-step chains, as suggested by Appendix A.8 .

sections.heading: Broader Impact.
sections.text: CDM opens both beneficial and potentially harmful applications. Distributional control can produce diverse and targeted outputs on complex models: for instance, the Stable Diffusion experiment (Section 5.3 ) demonstrates how MLGD-F can enforce demographic balance in generated portraits, a direct application to bias reduction. However, since 𝒢 \mathcal{G} is defined with great freedom, the same mechanism could be misused to deliberately steer frozen pipelines toward harmful distributions. Since MLGD-F operates on frozen models, existing safety mechanisms remain fully active.

sections.heading: A.8 Discussion
sections.text: The ECDF of L 2 L^{2} GMM across all 25 runs (Figure 4 ) summarises the dimension-dependent pattern: in 2D, MLGD-F achieves a lower mean L 2 L^{2} GMM while LGD shows higher spread (a mixture of better runs and worse runs); the two methods are comparable in 5D with LGD holding a slight edge on L 2 L^{2} GMM, and MLGD-F dominates in 10D. We conjecture this reflects two opposing error sources that scale differently with dimensionality, both identified formally in Appendix E . The distillation fidelity error ε s \varepsilon_{s} — the gap between the distilled sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} and the true conditional — is largely dimension-independent and acts as a fixed floor on MLGD-F’s solution quality. The gradient variance introduced by backpropagating through the K ⋆ K_{\star} -step unrolled diffusion chain worsens with depth and dimension [ 40 ] , and the single-step consistency model avoids this accumulation entirely. Notably, despite the consistency model’s lower conditional fidelity (Table 6 ), MLGD-F still matches or outperforms LGD in 10D, underscoring that gradient quality rather than sampler fidelity is the binding constraint at higher dimensionality — a point we return to in Appendix E . In low-to-intermediate dimensions the distillation error dominates, as seen in 5D, while in 10D the gradient variance term takes over and MLGD-F’s cleaner gradient graph becomes the decisive factor. The 5D setting is the approximate crossover between these two regimes.

sections.heading: B.1.1 Wasserstein Distance (WD)
sections.text: The Wasserstein distance [ 2 ] measures the minimum cost of transforming one probability distribution into another. For two probability distributions P P and Q Q on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , the 1-Wasserstein distance W 1 W_{1} is defined as: W 1 ​ ( P , Q ) = inf γ ∈ Γ ⁡ ( P , Q ) 𝔼 ( x , y ) ∼ γ ​ [ ‖ x − y ‖ 1 ] W_{1}(P,Q)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(P,Q)}\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\gamma}[\|x-y\|_{1}] (4) where Γ ⁡ ( P , Q ) \Gamma(P,Q) denotes the set of all joint distributions with marginals P P and Q Q . We include the 1D Wasserstein distance formulation here because the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD), described in the next section, reduces the high-dimensional problem to multiple 1D Wasserstein distance computations through random projections but in practice we will not use WD for higher dimensions in that work. For one-dimensional distributions P P and Q Q on ℝ \mathbb{R} , the 1-Wasserstein distance has a closed-form expression in terms of the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs): W 1 ​ ( P , Q ) = ∫ − ∞ ∞ | F P ​ ( x ) − F Q ​ ( x ) | ​ 𝑑 x W_{1}(P,Q)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|F_{P}(x)-F_{Q}(x)|\,dx (5) where F P F_{P} and F Q F_{Q} are the CDFs of P P and Q Q , respectively. sections.heading: B.1.2 Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD)
sections.text: We use the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD) [ 2 ] , which provides a computationally efficient approximation to the Wasserstein distance [ 2 ] in high dimensions. The SWD between distributions P P and Q Q is defined as: SWD ​ ( P , Q ) = ∫ 𝕊 d − 1 W 1 ​ ( π θ ​ # ​ P , π θ ​ # ​ Q ) ​ 𝑑 θ \text{SWD}(P,Q)=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}}W_{1}(\pi_{\theta}\#P,\pi_{\theta}\#Q)\,d\theta (7) where 𝕊 d − 1 \mathbb{S}^{d-1} is the unit sphere in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , π θ \pi_{\theta} denotes projection onto direction θ \theta , π θ ​ # ​ P \pi_{\theta}\#P and π θ ​ # ​ Q \pi_{\theta}\#Q are the distributions of the projected points along that direction, and W 1 W_{1} is the 1-Wasserstein distance. In practice, we approximate this integral by averaging the Wasserstein distance over L L random one-dimensional projections: SWD ​ ( P , Q ) ≈ 1 L ​ ∑ ℓ = 1 L W 1 ​ ( π θ ℓ ​ # ​ P , π θ ℓ ​ # ​ Q ) \text{SWD}(P,Q)\approx\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}W_{1}(\pi_{\theta_{\ell}}\#P,\pi_{\theta_{\ell}}\#Q) (8) where θ 1 , … , θ L \theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{L} are uniformly sampled from 𝕊 d − 1 \mathbb{S}^{d-1} . Notably, for one-dimensional data, SWD is equivalent to the 1-Wasserstein distance since the projection is the identity mapping, allowing us to use the same implementation for both metrics. in practice, when working with finite samples { x i } i = 1 n \{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} and { y j } j = 1 m \{y_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m} , we compute the 1-Wasserstein distance between the empirical 1D projections by sorting the projected points.

sections.heading: B.2 Dataset Construction
sections.text: We construct an augmented MNIST dataset that captures rotational ambiguity across digit classes.

sections.heading: B.2.1 Conditional Model
sections.text: For the conditional training the pipeline proceeds in two stages.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Logical-angle entries.
sections.text: We start from the standard MNIST training split (60,000 images). For each base image, we always retain a copy at logical angle 0 ​ ° 0° . We additionally include rotated copies at 90 ​ ° 90° , 180 ​ ° 180° , and 270 ​ ° 270° if a pretrained classifier assigns the rotated image to a digit class with confidence ≥ 0.9999 \geq 0.9999 . This threshold ensures that only genuinely rotationally ambiguous digits (e.g., “0”, “1”, “8”, “6”/“9”) contribute additional logical-angle entries. The classifier used is the dataset-construction CNN described below, trained on the standard MNIST training split.

sections.heading: Stage 2: Uniform random rotation.
sections.text: Each logical-angle entry is then rotated by a uniform random angle θ ∼ Uniform [ 0 ° , 360 ° ) \theta\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0°,360°) . The stored label angle is ( logical ​ _ ​ angle + θ ) mod 360 ​ ° ({\rm logical\_angle}+\theta)\bmod 360° . This produces a dataset of 82,483 samples with continuous, uniformly distributed rotation angles within each rotationally ambiguous class.

sections.heading: B.2.2 Unconditional Model
sections.text: The unconditional diffusion model is trained on a separate dataset consisting of all 70,000 MNIST images (train + test splits), each independently rotated by a uniform random angle at every epoch access, with no classifier filtering.

sections.heading: Dataset-construction classifier.
sections.text: This classifier is used only during dataset creation to determine which rotated copies of each digit are rotationally ambiguous. It is a three-block CNN trained on the standard MNIST training split for 15 epochs with batch size 128, Adam optimizer (lr = 10 − 3 =10^{-3} , weight decay = 10 − 4 =10^{-4} ), and learning-rate reduction on plateau (factor 0.5 0.5 , patience 2 2 ). Training augmentation consists of random rotation ( ± 10 ​ ° \pm 10° ), random affine transforms (translation up to 10%, scale 0.9 0.9 – 1.1 1.1 ), and standard MNIST normalisation ( μ = 0.1307 \mu=0.1307 , σ = 0.3081 \sigma=0.3081 ). Threshold for classification is 0.9999. The architecture is: • Block 1: Conv(1→32, 3×3) → BN → ReLU → Conv(32→32, 3×3) → BN → ReLU → MaxPool(2×2) → Dropout2D(0.25) • Block 2: Conv(32→64, 3×3) → BN → ReLU → Conv(64→64, 3×3) → BN → ReLU → MaxPool(2×2) → Dropout2D(0.25) • Block 3: Conv(64→128, 3×3) → BN → ReLU → MaxPool(2×2) → Dropout2D(0.25) • FC: Linear(1152→256) → BN → ReLU → Dropout(0.5) → Linear(256→128) → BN → ReLU → Dropout(0.5) → Linear(128→10)

sections.heading: Digit classifier (final results table).
sections.text: Since the recovered images x ∗ x^{*} may be arbitrarily rotated and are synthetically generated (and thus potentially lower in contrast than real MNIST digits), a classifier trained solely on standard upright MNIST would be unsuitable for evaluation. We therefore train a more robust variant designed to handle arbitrary orientations and mild image degradation. It shares the same three-block CNN backbone as the dataset-construction classifier, with three modifications for noise robustness: (i) an input Dropout2D(0.1) applied before the first convolution; (ii) a mid-block Dropout2D(0.1) inserted between the two convolutions in each of Blocks 1 and 2; and (iii) label smoothing ( ϵ = 0.1 \epsilon=0.1 ) in the cross-entropy loss during training. Training uses AdamW (lr = 10 − 3 =10^{-3} , weight decay = 10 − 4 =10^{-4} ) for 10 epochs with batch size 128. Training augmentation consists of random rotation ( ± 20 ​ ° \pm 20° ), random affine transforms (translation up to 10%, scale 0.9 0.9 – 1.1 1.1 ), Gaussian noise ( σ = 0.15 \sigma=0.15 ), and standard MNIST normalisation ( μ = 0.1307 \mu=0.1307 , σ = 0.3081 \sigma=0.3081 ). Threshold for classification is 0.7.

sections.heading: Conditional consistency model.
sections.text: The conditional model is an improved Consistency Training (iCT) model that predicts the rotation angle of an MNIST image as a circular ( cos ⁡ θ , sin ⁡ θ ) (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) vector, conditioned on the image. The image conditioning encoder is a two-block CNN that maps 28 × 28 28\times 28 images to a 128 128 -dimensional embedding, which is added to the noisy angle representation at each forward pass. The full architecture is: • Condition encoder: Conv(1→32, 3×3) → GroupNorm(8) → SiLU → Dropout2D(0.1) → Conv(32→32, 3×3) → GroupNorm(8) → SiLU → MaxPool(2×2) → Conv(32→64, 3×3) → GroupNorm(8) → SiLU → Dropout2D(0.15) → Conv(64→64, 3×3) → GroupNorm(8) → SiLU → MaxPool(2×2) → Dropout2D(0.2) → Flatten → Dropout(0.3) → Linear(3136→128) → SiLU • Input projection: Linear(2→128) → LayerNorm • Time embedding: Sinusoidal embedding (dim=128) • MLP backbone: 5 hidden layers of width 128 with ReLU activations • Output: LayerNorm → Linear(128→2), followed by iCT skip connection and ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization The output is normalized to the unit circle and decoded via θ ^ = atan2 ⁡ ( sin , cos ) mod 360 ​ ° \hat{\theta}=\mathrm{atan2}(\sin,\cos)\bmod 360° .

sections.heading: Where MLGD-F edits the scribble.
sections.text: Figure 8 contrasts the source scribble with the MLGD-F-optimized scribble, along with their pixel-wise | ⋅ | |\cdot| difference. The edits are spatially concentrated rather than diffuse: the largest modifications lie along the eye and eyebrow region and the lower hair outline. Most of the scribble is essentially unchanged; a minority of anatomically-meaningful contours account for the bulk of the edit magnitude. Yet even with the pixel-difference heatmap in hand, it remains unclear why these subtle edits suffice to shift the generated distribution toward a balanced male–female output. From a human perceptual standpoint, the changes are too small and too localized to constitute a legible gender signal. We hypothesize that MLGD-F has identified a structural sensitivity in the ControlNet–SDXL pipeline: a region of the conditioning space where small perturbations disproportionately influence the generative process, not because they are semantically meaningful to a human observer, but because the diffusion model’s internal representations are unexpectedly responsive to them. This points to a potential vulnerability in the underlying generative model — one that MLGD-F successfully exploits to achieve distributional control, but that also raises questions about the robustness and interpretability of ControlNet-based conditioning more broadly. sections.heading: Why those regions: gradient saliency.
sections.text: To test whether these edits are mechanistically meaningful rather than incidental, we ask which scribble pixels the CLIP gender signal is gradient-sensitive to, independent of what MLGD-F actually did. Define the per-pixel saliency as | ∂ s / ∂ x | |\partial s/\partial x| , where s ⁡ ( x ) = cos ⁡ ( CLIP ⁡ ( I ⁡ ( x ) ) , t man ) − cos ⁡ ( CLIP ⁡ ( I ⁡ ( x ) ) , t woman ) s(x)=\cos(\mathrm{CLIP}(I(x)),\,t_{\text{man}})-\cos(\mathrm{CLIP}(I(x)),\,t_{\text{woman}}) is the CLIP gender score of the image I ⁡ ( x ) I(x) generated from scribble x x , and t man , t woman t_{\text{man}},t_{\text{woman}} are the text embeddings of “a photo of a man”/“a photo of a woman”. The gradient is obtained by backpropagating s s from the generated image of the source scribble through the full differentiable pipeline (scribble → \to ControlNet-Scribble → \to VAE decoder → \to CLIP image encoder) and averaged over 20 20 random seeds to marginalise over sampler noise. Large saliency values indicate pixels whose local perturbation would most change the downstream gender score. We restrict the analysis to the line pixels of the source scribble, i.e. the non-background pixels of the input ( n = 33,828 n=33{,}828 ), since our question is whether, among the strokes that were actually drawn, the ones more predictive of the target attribute receive proportionally larger edits. Figure 9 shows the saliency map on the source scribble’s line support; the highest-saliency pixels concentrate on the hairline and the eye and eyebrow region, We quantify the alignment by binning line pixels by saliency magnitude and plotting the mean MLGD-F modification per bin (Figure 9 ). The relationship is monotone increasing with mild saturation at high saliency and Spearman ρ = 0.56 \rho=0.56 : pixels of the source stroke that the loss is more sensitive to receive proportionally larger edits. To investigate whether the concentration of edits on existing strokes is a structural artefact of the latent geometry rather than a purely semantic signal, we encoded both the source and MLGD-F-optimized scribbles through the VAE and computed, at each spatial position of the 64 × 64 64{\times}64 latent grid, the source latent norm (L2 norm across the four channels) and the edit magnitude (L2 norm of the latent difference). The two maps are positively correlated (Pearson r = 0.55 r=0.55 ), suggesting that a substantial portion of the edit concentration is explained by the fact that stroke pixels produce non-zero latent activations while background pixels do not — edits are suppressed in the background simply because there is little latent signal to perturb there. This does not invalidate the saliency finding, but it does suggest that the spatial concentration of MLGD-F edits is at least partly a consequence of the latent geometry: the optimiser can only meaningfully move in directions where the latent is already active. sections.heading: Takeaway.
sections.text: The two analyses together resolve the apparent paradox of small pixel edits producing a large distributional shift. Among the strokes of the source scribble, MLGD-F does not drift diffusely: it injects an aligned gradient signal that preferentially modifies the subset of strokes the downstream CLIP score is structurally sensitive to. This validates the inner estimator of Algorithm 2 as a mechanism rather than a black box: despite the long differentiable chain from scribble through ControlNet, VAE, and CLIP, the pulled-back gradient at each denoising step retains enough semantic structure to localise onto the anatomical features actually predictive of the target attribute. The regions identified — the eye, eyebrow, and hairline — are anatomically intuitive as gender-discriminative features. Yet from a human perceptual standpoint, the magnitude of the edits is strikingly small: changes that are nearly imperceptible to a human observer are sufficient to produce a substantial shift in the generated gender distribution. This disproportion between edit magnitude and distributional effect suggests a sensitivity in the underlying generative model that goes beyond what human perception would predict, and raises broader questions about the robustness of ControlNet-based conditioning to subtle input perturbations. The saliency analysis and latent correlation were computed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, with the saliency maps averaged over 20 20 random seeds. We report this analysis for the balanced target only; we expect the same mechanism in the skewed and continuum scenarios, but have not verified it quantitatively.

sections.heading: Appendix E Analysis of the MLGD-F Estimator
sections.text: This appendix analyses the plug-in loss estimator and the gradient estimator used inside the MLGD-F inner estimator (Algorithm 2 ; detailed form in Algorithm 3 ). The goal is to quantify how far the practical estimator is from the population quantity we would ideally optimize, and in particular to make explicit the two error sources introduced by the distilled conditional sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} : (i) the sample-level error ε s \varepsilon_{s} with which f ϕ f_{\phi} reproduces the true conditional, and (ii) the gradient error ε g \varepsilon_{g} with which the Jacobian of f ϕ f_{\phi} in the conditioning input x x matches the true reparameterising map (Proposition 2 ); a direct student-vs-teacher analogue is the subject of Proposition 3 , which ties the bounds to the memory argument of Section 5.4 : a K s K_{s} -step student replacing a K ⋆ K_{\star} -step teacher cuts reverse-mode graph depth by the ratio K ⋆ / K s K_{\star}/K_{s} at the cost of an additional student-teacher gradient discrepancy controlled by ε g , dist , ε dist \varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dist}} .

We can still measure a component of ε g \varepsilon_{g} against a differentiable multi-step reference sampler f ref f_{\mathrm{ref}} trained on the same data. Triangle inequality gives ε g ≤ ( 𝔼 η ​ ‖ ∂ x f ref − ∂ x f true ‖ F 2 ) 1 / 2 ⏟ ε g , d : open + ( 𝔼 η ​ ‖ ∂ x f ϕ − ∂ x f ref ‖ F 2 ) 1 / 2 ⏟ ε g , dist : measurable , \varepsilon_{g}\;\leq\;\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\|\partial_{x}f_{\mathrm{ref}}-\partial_{x}f_{\mathrm{true}}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}}_{\varepsilon_{g,d}\ :\ \text{open}}\;+\;\underbrace{\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\eta}\|\partial_{x}f_{\phi}-\partial_{x}f_{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{F}^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}}_{\varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}}\ :\ \text{measurable}}, where ε g , dist \varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}} is directly measurable by autograd under shared-noise coupling, while ε g , d \varepsilon_{g,d} remains unmeasurable for the same reason the output-level ε d \varepsilon_{d} (above) is not empirically verifiable: the truth’s Jacobian is unknown. The empirical check is one-sided . By triangle inequality, ε ^ g , dist \widehat{\varepsilon}_{g,\mathrm{dist}} can falsify Assumption 5 : a large measurement forces either ε g \varepsilon_{g} or ε g , d \varepsilon_{g,d} to be large. But a small ε ^ g , dist \widehat{\varepsilon}_{g,\mathrm{dist}} does not prove ε g \varepsilon_{g} is small, because f ϕ f_{\phi} and f ref f_{\mathrm{ref}} may share systematic biases and be jointly far from truth in the Jacobian without being far from each other. sections.heading: Open questions.
sections.text: Several questions remain open. First, what prompt-level properties predict Jacobian instability: 16 outliers across 100 prompts show no obvious syntactic or semantic pattern, though one plausible explanation is mode mismatch — prompts that elicit visually different outputs from teacher and student may induce larger Jacobian discrepancies, since the two models effectively compute gradients around different local modes of the image distribution. Second, whether the strong alignment observed for photo / cinematic reflects an inductive bias of SDXL-Lightning towards photorealistic outputs, which would imply that the choice of distillation target distribution matters for downstream gradient-based use of the student. We leave these to future work.

sections.heading: E.10 Discussion
sections.text: The propositions above clarify three conceptual points that are specific to the CDM setting and do not follow from generic stochastic-gradient theory: • The gradient oracle used inside MLGD-F is a compound estimator; its error decomposes cleanly into a finite-sample variance term, a sampler-output bias ( ε s \varepsilon_{s} ), and a sampler-Jacobian bias ( ε g \varepsilon_{g} ). The U-statistic estimator is unbiased in the finite-sample sense, so finite sampling enters Proposition 2 only through variance, not through bias; the corresponding loss-side Monte Carlo term lives in Proposition 1 . • The distillation error enters both the loss and its gradient linearly in ε s \varepsilon_{s} , via the Lipschitz relation MMD ⁡ ( 𝒫 ϕ , 𝒫 ) ≤ L k ​ W 1 ​ ( 𝒫 ϕ , 𝒫 ) \operatorname{MMD}(\mathcal{P}_{\phi},\mathcal{P})\leq L_{k}\,W_{1}(\mathcal{P}_{\phi},\mathcal{P}) and the L 2 L^{2} coupling of Assumption 2 . This is sharper than a TV-based bound and is specific to characteristic-kernel distributional losses: point-target inverse design ( ‖ f ⁡ ( x ) − y ⋆ ‖ \|f(x)-y^{\star}\| ) has no analogous distributional stability property. • The memory advantage of the distilled sampler comes at an analytically quantifiable student-teacher gradient discrepancy O ⁡ ( ε g , dist + ε dist ) O(\varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dist}}) , supporting the interpretation of the 43 43\, GB vs 375 375\, GB comparison in Section 5.4 as quantitatively analysed (rather than merely empirical) by Proposition 3 . Assumption 5 is the only assumption not routinely available from the consistency-model literature. A formal analysis of Jacobian-level distillation guarantees is a natural direction for future work.

sections.heading: The bound is qualitative, not numerical.
sections.text: Empirically, the Jacobian gap r ^ g \hat{r}_{g} exceeds the output gap r ^ s \hat{r}_{s} across all style groups (Table 18 ). Without outliers (Panel B), r ^ g / r ^ s \hat{r}_{g}/\hat{r}_{s} ranges from 2.39 × 2.39\times ( photo ) to 4.05 × 4.05\times ( cartoon ), with an overall ratio of 4.34 × 4.34\times ; outlier prompts can push this to 33.31 × 33.31\times (Panel A). Proposition 2 ’s bound is therefore qualitatively informative — it identifies the right two error sources and shows the gradient bias decomposes cleanly into them — but not quantitatively tight at current distillation quality. We view the propositions as a framework for measurement and regime identification: they tell us which quantities to estimate and how they propagate, rather than supplying numerical guarantees on the algorithm. More broadly, this points to a gap in the theory of model distillation itself. Standard distillation analyses, and the training objectives that flow from them, control output fidelity : L 2 L^{2} or Wasserstein closeness between student and teacher. This is the right bound when the distilled model is used as a function evaluator . MLGD-F, by contrast, uses f ϕ f_{\phi} as an autograd oracle : its Jacobian is consumed, not just its values. Whenever a distilled or compressed model is deployed in a downstream optimisation rather than a downstream evaluation (MLGD-F, bi-level optimisation with learned inner solvers, differentiable simulators, gradient-guided inverse design in general), output-fidelity distillation bounds are insufficient, and an ε g \varepsilon_{g} -type Jacobian-fidelity guarantee is required. Current consistency-model training provides the former but not the latter.

However, many design goals are naturally distributional rather than pointwise, incorporating the inherent uncertainty of Y Y and targeting a specific form for it, a task not addressed by standard inverse design. To address this issue we introduce Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM) 1 1 1 The phrase ”conditional distribution matching” is also used in the domain-adaptation literature [ 41 ] with a different meaning (aligning source and target conditionals across datasets); our use is an inverse-design problem over a fixed generative process. See Section 3 for details. , a new inverse-design problem class in generative modeling: given a joint distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{P}(X,Y) and a target distribution 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) , find an input x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . We formally define two variants: Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (CDMS) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (CDMO). To solve these problems, we propose MLGD-F ( Matching-Loss Guided Diffusion with a Fast inner sampler ), a plug-and-play inference-time algorithm that combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler, requiring no additional training or fine-tuning. By leveraging single-step conditional sampling, MLGD-F enables tractable gradient computation, making the estimation of 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) both memory-efficient and computationally lightweight. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic benchmarks, structured image transformations, and generative editing optimization, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank supports. 1 Introduction Generative models have emerged as a cornerstone of modern machine learning, achieving remarkable results in image synthesis, voice generation, and time-series modeling [ 19 , 43 , 39 ] . The paradigm has evolved from unconditional generation , learning to sample from an unknown data distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) [ 33 , 16 , 34 ] , toward increasingly controlled generation. Conditional generation allows sampling x 0 ∼ 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ∣ Y = y ) x_{0}\sim\mathcal{P}(X\mid Y=y) for a user-specified label y y [ 9 , 17 ] , loss-guided methods [ 6 , 35 ] generate samples that minimize a given objective ℒ : 𝒳 → ℝ \mathcal{L}:\mathcal{X}	o\mathbb{R} while remaining faithful to the data distribution. A natural instantiation of loss-guided generation is inverse design : find an input x x such that a forward learned model f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) is close to a desired point output y ∗ y^{*} [ 31 ] , successfully applied in protein engineering [ 8 ] and drug discovery [ 13 ] . However, this paradigm is inherently limited to point targets: it cannot express goals where the desired outcome is a distribution over outputs rather than a single value. In many modern settings the mapping from input to output is mediated by a complex generative process 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) that we cannot modify: a pretrained diffusion model with billions of parameters, a physical process such as protein folding, or a black-box simulator. The only lever the user controls is the input x x . Classical inverse design uses this lever to match a specific target output y ∗ y^{*} : find x x such that f ⁡ ( x ) ≈ y ∗ f(x)\approx y^{*} . In many applications, however, the desired outcome is not a single value but a distribution over outcomes, for instance, an amino acid sequence x x such that 𝒫 ⁡ ( structure ∣ X = x ) ≈ 1 2 ​ δ A + 1 2 ​ δ B \mathcal{P}(	ext{structure}\mid X=x)\approx rac{1}{2}\delta_{A}+ rac{1}{2}\delta_{B} for two target folds A A and B B [ 15 ] , generative pipelines whose outputs are balanced across demographic groups, or design tasks that require diverse but constrained outputs. We address the more general distributional inverse-design problem: accept any frozen 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) , optimise the controllable input x x , and target a user-specified distribution 𝒢 \mathcal{G} over Y Y rather than a point y ∗ y^{*} , without relying on domain-specific scoring functions. Our contributions. 1. Problem formulation. We define two problems, Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling (Problem 1 ) and Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization (Problem 2 ), which move beyond characterizing samples by their own properties, instead seeking x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) . 2. Algorithm. MLGD-F combines a pretrained score-based diffusion model with a pretrained fast conditional sampler to enable tractable gradient-based optimisation through single-step conditional sampling, operating entirely at inference time with no fine-tuning. 3. Empirical validation. We validate MLGD-F on synthetic Mixture of Gaussians, an MNIST rotation task, and a large-scale Stable Diffusion image editing pipeline, demonstrating recovery of inputs whose induced conditional distributions match user-specified targets. 2 Problem Formulation We consider a joint distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( X , Y ) \mathcal{P}(X,Y) over paired random variables, where X X denotes a variable of interest and Y Y an associated variable. Let ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denote a distance metric between probability distributions (e.g., the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, MMD, or the Sliced Wasserstein Distance, SWD). Problem 1 (Conditional Distribution Matching Sampling) . Given a target distribution 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) , the ideal target is the tilted distribution 𝒬 β ​ ( x ) ∝ 𝒫 ⁡ ( x ) ​ e − β ​ ℒ ​ ( x ) , where ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ , \mathcal{Q}_{ eta}(x)\propto\mathcal{P}(x)\,e^{- eta\,\mathcal{L}(x)},\quad	ext{where}\quad\mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\|, with β ≥ 0  eta\!\geq\!0 an inverse temperature interpolating between the prior ( β = 0  eta\!=\!0 ) and the optimum of ℒ \mathcal{L} ( β → ∞  eta\!	o\!\infty ). Exact sampling from 𝒬 β \mathcal{Q}_{ eta} requires an intractable noisy-time guidance score; our algorithm (Section 4 ) provides an LGD-style approximate sampler, analysed in Remark 2 of Appendix E . Problem 2 (Conditional Distribution Matching Optimization) . Find input x ∗ x^{*} that minimizes the distance between the induced conditional distribution and the target: x ∗ ≡ arg ⁡ min x ​ ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ . x^{*}\;\equiv\;\arg\min_{x}\;\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\|. Problem 2 corresponds to Problem 1 in the limit β → ∞  eta	o\infty , where 𝒬 ⁡ ( x ) \mathcal{Q}(x) concentrates at the mode of the loss. Both problems are instances of loss-guided sampling [ 35 ] specialised to the distributional loss ℒ ⁡ ( x ) = ‖ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ) − 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) ‖ \mathcal{L}(x)=\|\mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x)-\mathcal{G}(Y)\| . 3 Background and Related Work Diffusion models. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [ 33 , 16 ] define a forward process that gradually adds Gaussian noise to data x 0 x_{0} over T T steps, producing a sequence x 0 , x 1 , … , x T x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{T} , and learn a reverse process that denoises x T ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) back to a sample x 0 x_{0} from the data distribution. Throughout we use this notation: x t x_{t} is the noisy state at timestep t t ; the forward marginal has the closed form q ⁡ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = α ¯ t ​ x 0 + 1 − α ¯ t ​ ϵ q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=\sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0}+\sqrt{1- ar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and noise schedule { α ¯ t } t = 1 T \{ ar{\alpha}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} ; s θ ​ ( x t , t ) s_{	heta}(x_{t},t) denotes the learned score network of the unconditional model for 𝒫 ⁡ ( X ) \mathcal{P}(X) ; and x ^ 0 = ( x t + ( 1 − α ¯ t ) ​ s θ ​ ( x t , t ) ) / α ¯ t \hat{x}_{0}\!=\!(x_{t}+(1- ar{\alpha}_{t})s_{	heta}(x_{t},t))/\sqrt{ ar{\alpha}_{t}} is Tweedie’s estimate of the clean sample given x t x_{t} . Score-based models [ 38 ] provide a unifying SDE framework for this family. A deterministic alternative to ancestral sampling is the probability flow ODE (used via the DDIM sampler [ 34 ] ), which traces a deterministic trajectory through the same marginals and enables faster sampling with fewer steps. Few-step diffusion models. Standard diffusion models require 30 30 – 1000 1000 sequential denoising steps at inference time [ 16 , 34 ] , motivating research into faster inference strategies. One direction is consistency models [ 36 , 37 ] , which enforce self-consistency along the probability-flow ODE trajectory without requiring a pretrained teacher. Another direction is diffusion distillation , which compresses a pretrained diffusion model into a student that generates samples in one or very few steps [ 30 , 32 ] . We exploit the single-step property common to both families to make inner-loop conditional sampling tractable at every denoising step of the outer diffusion process. Loss-guided sampling. Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) [ 6 ] and Loss-Guided Diffusion (LGD) [ 35 ] modify the reverse diffusion process by incorporating gradient information from a differentiable loss function ℒ ⁡ ( x 0 ) \mathcal{L}(x_{0}) . At each denoising step, the score is augmented by ∇ x t ℒ ​ ( x ^ 0 ) 
abla_{x_{t}}\mathcal{L}(\hat{x}_{0}) , where x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} is an estimate of the clean sample obtained via Tweedie’s formula. LGD further stabilises the gradient by averaging over multiple Monte Carlo Tweedie estimates. This framework enables flexible, zero-shot guidance for a wide range of objectives without retraining the generative prior. Distribution matching. A large family of generative methods trains a parametric generator so that its output distribution matches a target 𝒢 \mathcal{G} , using losses based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy [ 22 , 21 ] , Optimal Transport / Sinkhorn divergences [ 12 ] , These approaches require differentiating through the generator and updating its weights, making them expensive and target-specific: a new 𝒢 \mathcal{G} requires retraining. Our setting is orthogonal: the generative pipeline (both the diffusion prior and the conditional model f ϕ f_{\phi} ) is frozen , and we instead optimise a single input x ∗ x^{*} such that 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches 𝒢 \mathcal{G} . No generator weights are updated, no target-specific training is required, and the method operates entirely at inference time. Terminological note. The phrase "conditional distribution matching" has prior unrelated uses. In the domain-adaptation literature [ 41 ] it refers to aligning the source and target conditionals 𝒫 src ​ ( X ∣ Y ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{src}}(X\mid Y) and 𝒫 tgt ​ ( X ∣ Y ) \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{tgt}}(X\mid Y) across two datasets so that a classifier learned on one transfers to the other. In concurrent work on discrete-diffusion distillation [ 11 ] it refers to a training objective in which a student model is trained to match a pretrained teacher’s reverse conditional transitions. Our use is unrelated to either: we study the inverse-design problem of finding an input x ∗ x^{*} whose induced conditional 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) , with a single fixed generative process. The memory gap is formalised by Proposition 3 in Appendix E : the few-step student reduces reverse-mode graph depth by the step-count ratio K ⋆ / K s K_{\star}/K_{s} , with the resulting student-teacher gradient discrepancy controlled by the additional distillation errors O ⁡ ( ε g , dist + ε dist ) O(\varepsilon_{g,\mathrm{dist}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{dist}}) . Architectural Parity and Scaling. To isolate the impact of the denoising step count, we observe that our setup utilizes an identical architectural backbone across both configurations: the UNet ( ≈ \approx 2.6B parameters), ControlNet [ 44 ] , and CLIP text encoders [ 29 ] remain constant. Notably, SDXL-Turbo is obtained by distilling SDXL-Base with the architecture unchanged - the two models differ only in their weights, not their structure [ 32 ] . Consequently, the computational cost of a single forward pass is equivalent across both, and all observed differences in memory and speed are a direct consequence of the denoising step count alone. The observed differences in memory and speed are thus a direct consequence of the computation graph depth. Since SDXL Base requires K ⋆ = 30 K_{\star}=30 steps for high-quality reconstruction compared to K s = 2 K_{s}=2 for SDXL Turbo, the resulting gradient graph is fundamentally 15 × 15	imes deeper. To manage memory, one can employ gradient checkpointing ; however, while this technique avoids storing intermediate activations, the overhead of maintaining the computation graph nodes for each of the K K denoising steps still scales linearly with the number of iterations. This order-of-magnitude reduction transforms MLGD-F into a tractable tool for iterative research and deployment. 6 Conclusion We introduced Conditional Distribution Matching (CDM) , a new problem class that generalizes inverse design to the distributional setting. Rather than seeking an input x x that produces a specific output y ∗ y^{*} , CDM seeks an input x ∗ x^{*} whose entire induced conditional distribution 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X = x ∗ ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X=x^{*}) matches a user-specified target 𝒢 ⁡ ( Y ) \mathcal{G}(Y) . To our knowledge, this problem class has not been explicitly studied before. We formalized two variants, CDMS and CDMO, and introduced MLGD-F to solve them at inference time without any training or fine-tuning. A central advantage of the plug-and-play design is that MLGD-F directly inherits quality gains from improvements in the underlying pretrained models: as stronger diffusion priors and few-step conditional samplers become available, optimization quality improves automatically. The few-step model is essential for tractability: as demonstrated in Section 5.4 , replacing a single-step sampler with a standard multi-step diffusion model increases peak memory by nearly an order of magnitude and runtime from hours to days, rendering the method infeasible at scale. Empirically, we validated MLGD-F across settings of increasing scale and complexity, from synthetic Mixture of Gaussians, through an MNIST rotation task, to a large-scale Stable Diffusion image editing pipeline, demonstrating reliable recovery of inputs whose induced conditional distributions match diverse user-specified targets, including discrete mixtures and continuous low-rank submanifolds. Limitations. Optimization quality is bounded by the fidelity of the pretrained distilled model — if the conditional sampler f ϕ f_{\phi} poorly approximates 𝒫 ⁡ ( Y ∣ X ) \mathcal{P}(Y\mid X) , the guidance gradient will be biased regardless of the number of runs. The stochastic nature of the inner-loop loss estimation means multiple independent runs are often needed to find a good solution, which multiplies the compute cost. Runtime at large scale may be prohibitive for latency-sensitive applications. Finally, the method currently requires the conditional model to be differentiable end-to-end with respect to the input x x ; non-differentiable or black-box conditional models would require gradient-free extensions. Future Work. CDM opens a research direction of optimizing over induced conditional distributions, one we hope will inspire dedicated solvers, tighter theoretical guarantees, and new application domains. This work focuses on continuous input spaces; an important direction is extending CDM to discrete spaces.
